stories.title: 'So why should he be dragged into it?': State House says Hichilema will not comment on term limits, as Lubinda demands he rule out benefiting and Musumali calls silence endorsement
stories.excerpt: Two days after the Justice Minister left three term-limit petitions to Parliament, State House spoke for itself on Sunday 15 November. Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the debate belongs to citizens, that the President is focused on development, and that those demanding a comment would cry foul if he gave one. Former PF vice-president Given Lubinda has challenged Hichilema to distance himself from a third term; Socialist Party general secretary Cosmas Musumali calls standing aside indirect endorsement; GEARS wants a referendum.

image.label: The President's silence
image.caption: State House says the term-limit debate came from citizens and the President will not be drawn; his critics say that is the problem.

body: The argument over Zambia's two-term presidential limit has now drawn a statement from State House itself, and it is a refusal to take part. In a written statement issued in Lusaka on Sunday 15 November, Clayson Hamasaka, the Chief Government Communications Specialist at State House, said President Hakainde Hichilema would not comment on the debate about removing Article 106(3) from the Constitution, because his attention is on development and on reducing poverty. The statement was reported by the Zambia Monitor and carried in full by the Zambian Observer, and News Diggers reported it on Monday 16 November alongside the opposition reaction.

Hamasaka's central point was that the campaign did not start in government. **"This debate is coming from the citizens,"** he said in the statement, adding: **"So why should he be dragged into it?"** He asked what the President's critics expected him to say, and argued that if Hichilema spoke they would accuse him of restricting free expression, while the Zambian Observer's text of the statement has him saying that it would be dictatorial for a head of state to curb a constitutionally guaranteed freedom. In the Observer's account he described the attempts to pull the President into the row as unfair and as political mischief, and said Hichilema would continue to uphold the Constitution and the rule of law.

The statement then turned to the government's programme. Hamasaka said the President was concentrating on the Grow Zambia Agenda and its core targets, and named El Niño, food security and energy security as the immediate priorities, urging Zambians to unite behind the agenda rather than the constitutional argument.

body.text: What the critics want to hear

body: The statement answers a specific demand. News Diggers reported on Monday that Given Lubinda, the former vice-president of the Patriotic Front and a former justice minister, had challenged Hichilema to state his position on the removal of term limits and to assure Zambians that he would not be the beneficiary of any change. In an interview on Friday 13 November, according to the paper, Lubinda said that if the limit were ever removed the change should take effect only after the 2031 elections and should be put to a national referendum. The Zambian Observer, in a report on Saturday 14 November of a Facebook post by Lubinda, quoted him arguing that a parliamentary majority is not the same as the will of the people: **"The will of the people must be demonstrated, not merely declared,"** he wrote, and he pointed to Frederick Chiluba's rejection of a third-term campaign in 2001 as the precedent the President should follow. Opposition leaders and civil society groups have been asking Hichilema for his position.

Dr Cosmas Musumali, the general secretary of the Socialist Party, went further. Responding to a News Diggers press query on Saturday 14 November, he said that by declaring it would not interfere with the petitions the government had indirectly endorsed them, and he called the claim of non-interference **"a textbook exercise in political deflection"**. In the same report, Luckson Lungu, the board chairperson of the GEARS Initiative, said the removal of presidential term limits should be subject to a referendum rather than left to Parliament alone.

The exchange follows the press briefing on Friday 13 November at which Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu said three petitions asking the National Assembly to remove Article 106(3), the two-term limit, had been submitted by members of the public, political leaders and civil society organisations, that the government would not interfere, and that the Assembly was the appropriate institution to consider them, as the Times of Zambia and News Diggers reported. The Zambian Observer's account of Sunday's statement recalled that the petitions have been promoted by some UPND supporters, including nominated members of Parliament, who cite the President's record, while opposition parties, church bodies and civil society groups have warned that removing the limit could weaken Zambia's democracy.

Not every intervention at the weekend was for or against the petitions as drafted. The Zambian Observer on Sunday 15 November carried remarks by the economist Dr Lubinda Haabazoka suggesting that Zambia should consider cutting the presidential term from five years to four, rather than discussing a longer one, and testing whether the ruling party would accept that alternative. Zambia has had a five-year presidential term since independence in 1964.

body.title: Who has said what
items: Friday 13 November — Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu: three petitions; government will not interfere; Parliament decides.
Friday 13 and Saturday 14 November — Given Lubinda (PF): the President should state his position and distance himself from a third term; any change after 2031 and by referendum.
Saturday 14 November — Cosmas Musumali (Socialist Party): non-interference is indirect endorsement. Luckson Lungu (GEARS): put it to a referendum.
Sunday 15 November — Clayson Hamasaka (State House): the debate is the citizens'; the President will not comment.

body.confirmed: State House issued a statement on Sunday 15 November, in the name of Clayson Hamasaka, saying the President will not comment on the term-limit debate; the Zambia Monitor, the Zambian Observer and News Diggers all reported it. Lubinda's challenge was reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer; Musumali's response and the GEARS call for a referendum by News Diggers. Mwiimbu's Friday briefing, and the three petitions, were reported by the Times of Zambia and News Diggers.
body.unverified: Whether President Hichilema would sign an amendment if Parliament passed one is unknown: State House has declined to say, and the reports of the Justice Minister's Friday briefing do not record his personal position. How many signatures the three petitions carry, and when the National Assembly will consider them, has not been reported.

stories.title: Killed before dawn on the Mwinilunga road: Kalumbila District Commissioner Brenda Sankisa and her driver die as a government Hilux hits a truck's trailer
stories.excerpt: Police say the Kalumbila District Commissioner and her driver died at about 05:00 on Sunday 15 November when their Toyota Hilux ran into the rear trailer of a truck on the Mutanda–Mwinilunga Road, in Chief Mumena's area about 15 kilometres south of the Mutanda checkpoint. A district messenger travelling with them was injured. The UPND's Kalumbila constituency leadership announced the death on party platforms before the police statement.

image.label: Mutanda–Mwinilunga Road
image.caption: A district commissioner and her driver died on the road to Mwinilunga early on Sunday; a third passenger survived.

body: The District Commissioner for Kalumbila, Brenda Sankisa, and her driver were killed early on Sunday 15 November when the government vehicle they were travelling in struck the back of a truck on the Mutanda–Mwinilunga Road in North-Western Province. News Diggers reported the police account, and the Zambian Observer carried the first notice of her death from the ruling party's constituency leadership.

According to the police public relations officer Chipo Kaitisha, quoted by News Diggers, the crash happened at about 05:00 in the Kambazhi area, roughly 15 kilometres south of the Mutanda security checkpoint, in Chief Mumena's area. The Toyota Hilux, registration GRZ 817DF and belonging to Kalumbila District, hit the rear trailer of a truck. Both the commissioner and the driver died. A third occupant, described as a district messenger, survived with bruises to both hands and legs. The police statement opened by recording that officers in Kalumbila had logged a fatal road traffic accident that day; the rest of the account, including the truck's details and the condition of the road, sits behind the paper's paywall and has not been reported elsewhere.

The Zambian Observer reported on Sunday that the news had emerged through the United Party for National Development's Kalumbila constituency structures, in a notice issued by the constituency secretary, Richard Masuwa, which referred to the commissioner as Mama Brenda Sankisa Kamboyi and said more information would follow. The Observer said the accident had first been reported by North West TV and that at the time of its report the Zambia Police Service had not issued an official statement; the police account carried by News Diggers followed later in the day.

The two accounts agree on the essentials and differ in small ways. The Observer's notice, drawn from the party, gives the commissioner's name as Brenda Sankisa Kamboyi; the police account carried by News Diggers calls her Brenda Sankisa. The Observer places the crash at Kambanji and News Diggers at Kambazhi, both describing the same stretch of the Mutanda–Mwinilunga Road. The police put the time at about 05:00, before daylight, and said the government vehicle ran into the rear of a truck's trailer, which is consistent with the Observer's description of a road traffic accident that morning.

What neither report gives is the driver's name, the cause of the collision, whether the truck was moving or parked, or whether its driver has been detained or charged. No funeral arrangements had been announced by Sunday evening, and the party's notice said only that more information would follow. A fuller police statement may answer those questions; the version News Diggers published is cut off after the vehicle's registration, and the Observer reported that the police had not yet spoken when it published.

body.confirmed: Police confirmed, through their public relations officer, that the Kalumbila District Commissioner and her driver died at about 05:00 on Sunday 15 November when their Toyota Hilux hit a truck's trailer on the Mutanda–Mwinilunga Road, and that a district messenger was injured (News Diggers). The UPND's Kalumbila constituency secretary announced the death (Zambian Observer).
body.unverified: The cause of the collision, the identity of the driver, the condition of the truck driver and any action against him have not been reported. The full police statement is behind a paywall.

stories.title: 'Especially our children': in Choma Central SDA, Hichilema tells MPs and councillors that public office exists to improve lives, and leaves a gift the papers count differently
stories.excerpt: On the second day of his Southern Province visit, President Hichilema and the First Lady attended a service at Choma Central Seventh-day Adventist Church on Saturday 14 November. He told office-holders to make sure children get the benefit of free education, school feeding and the scrapping of exam fees, and said leaders should read the church's messages carefully. The Times of Zambia reports a K100,000 gift to the congregation; News Diggers puts the First Family's contribution to the building project at K200,000.

image.label: Choma, Saturday
image.caption: The President used a church service in Choma to remind elected officials what their offices are for.

body: A day after his rally in Choma, President Hakainde Hichilema spent Saturday 14 November in church in the same town, and used the pulpit to address the politicians in the pews. At Choma Central Seventh-day Adventist Church, with First Lady Mutinta Hichilema beside him, he said that those who hold public office sought it in order to work for the people and improve their lives, and that children in particular must feel the benefit. The service was reported by the Times of Zambia and by News Diggers.

According to the Times, the President said the government is committed to prioritising the welfare and education of children across the country, and that public leaders must ensure children benefit from free education, the school feeding programme and the cancellation of examination fees. **"Those of us in public office must continue working tirelessly for our people, especially our children,"** he said. He addressed members of Parliament, mayors, council chairpersons and councillors directly, asking them to stay committed to serving the people and to make sure government policies change the lives of ordinary citizens.

News Diggers reported the President saying that office-holders should discern and correctly interpret the messages they hear from the church so that they can serve citizens diligently, and the Times reported him praising the congregation's message as holding lessons for people in leadership. He urged leaders to understand the environment in which they operate and to read between the lines before taking decisions. He opened, in News Diggers' account, by saying he did not have much to say beyond a few things.

The two papers agree on the message and differ on the money. The Times of Zambia reported that the President donated K100,000 to the congregation. News Diggers reported that the President and the First Family had donated K200,000 towards the church's building project. No State House figure had been published by Monday morning, so both are given here as reported.

The service followed a community engagement in Choma on Friday 13 November at which, News Diggers reported, the President dismissed talk that the UPND was losing popularity by pointing to its clean sweep of the 14 seats contested in the 5 November by-elections, promised a dual carriageway from Lusaka to Southern Province on the model of the Lusaka–Ndola road, and warned teachers and nurses who refuse rural postings that they risk their jobs. It preceded by a day the State House statement in which his spokesman said he would not be drawn into the argument over presidential term limits because his focus is on delivering development. The church address, with its emphasis on free education and school feeding, was in the same register: a government listing what it says it has done for ordinary families.

stories.title: Twenty arrests at a suspended gold site, a deportation after a shooting and 15 held over permits: the State moves on Mpika's informal gold rush
stories.excerpt: The Minerals Regulation Commission said on Sunday 15 November that 16 Chinese nationals and four Zambians had been arrested at Muneshi Stream in Chief Mukungule's area of Mpika, where it says mining resumed two months after it suspended the site and the stream is suspected to have been polluted and blocked. Separately, the Immigration Department deported a Somali national on Friday 13 November over a shooting at a gold plant in Kanyelele, and held ten Chinese and five Tanzanians for allegedly working without permits.

image.label: Muneshi Stream
image.caption: Regulators say a gold site they shut two months ago was back in operation, with the stream polluted and blocked.

body: Three arms of the State acted against Mpika's informal gold trade in the space of a weekend. The Minerals Regulation Commission (MRC) announced on Sunday 15 November that 16 Chinese nationals and four Zambians had been arrested for allegedly mining and processing gold without licences at Muneshi Stream, in Chief Mukungule's area of Mpika District, Muchinga Province. The announcement was reported by the Zambia Monitor and, via Kalemba, by the Zambian Observer. News Diggers reported the same day that the Immigration Department had deported a Somali man over a shooting at a gold processing plant elsewhere in the district and detained 15 foreign workers at two mines.

The MRC's statement, issued in Lusaka and attributed by the Zambia Monitor to Malfred Moolela, its Manager for Minerals Security and Protection, said the arrests were made with the Zambia Environmental Management Agency and state security wings. The alleged offences are mining and processing gold without the required licences or authorisations, suspected pollution of the stream with unidentified substances, and obstruction of its natural flow, which the Commission says has limited water access for communities downstream. According to Moolela, the Commission had suspended mining and processing at the same site about two months earlier, and the activity had carried on regardless. The Zambian Observer reported the Commission warning that it would take decisive action against individuals and companies that break mining and environmental law. Neither report says what charges, if any, have been laid, or whether the 20 remain in custody.

The Immigration Department's action concerns a different site. In a statement reported by News Diggers, the department's chief public relations officer, Namati Nshinka, said a 50-year-old Somali national had been deported on Friday 13 November through Kenneth Kaunda International Airport for discharging a firearm during a dispute at Empiric Trading Limited, a gold processing facility in the Kanyelele area of Mpika. In the same statement the department said ten Chinese and five Tanzanian nationals had been apprehended for allegedly working without valid employment permits at two mines, in Shiwang'andu and Mpika districts respectively. Lusaka Brief is not naming the deported man, who has not been charged before a court; the rest of the statement is behind the paper's paywall.

body.text: Formalisation and enforcement, side by side

body: The arrests follow a stakeholder meeting in Mpika on which the Zambia Monitor reported on Thursday 12 November, where the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development and the MRC began formalising artisanal mining at Kamambwe, Kanyelele and Danger Hill. In a speech read for him by Moolela, the MRC's Director General, Tom Hara, said informal operators at the identified sites had been told to leave so that the sites could be demarcated and tenements allocated to eligible artisanal miners, and he cited Section 20(5) of the Minerals Regulation Act No. 14 of 2024, which reserves artisanal mining rights for Zambian citizens subject to the Commission's approval. Muchinga's deputy permanent secretary, Grant Chisapa, warned at the meeting about mercury use and the risk to water sources and to the North Luangwa ecosystem, while Chief Chikwanda of Mpika welcomed the consultation of local miners before tenements are allocated.

body.confirmed: The MRC announced the arrest of 16 Chinese nationals and four Zambians at Muneshi Stream (Zambia Monitor; Zambian Observer via Kalemba). The Immigration Department announced the deportation of a Somali national and the apprehension of ten Chinese and five Tanzanian nationals (News Diggers). The formalisation exercise was reported by the Zambia Monitor on 12 November.
body.unverified: The allegations of unlicensed mining and pollution are the Commission's; none of the 20 has been reported as charged, and no response from them or from the companies involved has been published. The quantity of gold or equipment seized, if any, has not been reported.

stories.title: Plant in Kawambwa, wait in Lusaka: the Met Department's first bulletin of the season clears ten northern districts to sow, tells 42 to hold off and warns of a short southern season
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Meteorological Department's first agrometeorological bulletin of 2026/27, covering 13 to 26 November and reported by the Zambia Monitor, puts the country at a yellow 'Get Ready' level. Rain since 1 October stands at 125% of the long-term average in Northern Province and 110% in Luapula, but only 63% in Southern, 53% in Lusaka and 52% in Central. Ten Luapula, Northern and North-Western districts may plant now; all of Lusaka and Southern and most of Central and Eastern are told to wait, with little rain expected before 26 November.

image.label: Rain since 1 October
image.caption: The north has had more rain than usual and the south about half; the Met Department's planting advice follows the same line.

body: Zambia's rainy season has started, but only in the north, and the Meteorological Department's first planting advisory of the year tells most of the country to keep its seed in the bag. The Zambia Monitor reported on Sunday 15 November on the department's first Agrometeorological Bulletin of the 2026/27 season, which covers the fortnight from 13 to 26 November and places the country at a yellow advisory level, labelled Get Ready. The El Niño warning behind it has been building since October, when News Diggers reported the department urging farmers to spread their risk across drought-tolerant crops.

The bulletin's rainfall figures, as reported by the Monitor, show how uneven the start has been. Measured against the 1991 to 2020 average, rain since 1 October has reached 125% of normal in Northern Province and 110% in Luapula, but 72% on the Copperbelt, 63% in Southern, 53% in Lusaka and 52% in Central. Soils are dry almost everywhere: as of 10 November only six northern districts had moist soil, and seven Copperbelt districts had received between 9 and 13 millimetres in the first ten days of the month.

The department's rule, according to the Monitor's account, is that a farmer should plant only when three conditions are met at once: at least 40 millimetres of rain over the preceding one to two weeks, soil moisture to a depth of about 15 centimetres, and a two-week forecast with no dry spell longer than ten days. On that basis ten districts are cleared to plant now or with the next rain: Chiengi, Chipili, Kawambwa, Mwansabombwe and Nchelenge in Luapula; Kaputa, Lunte and Mporokoso in Northern; and Ikelenge and Mwinilunga in North-Western. Sixteen more, including Kasama, Mansa, Mbala and Kasempa, should plant after the next good rain. The seven Copperbelt districts of Chililabombwe, Chingola, Kitwe, Luanshya, Masaiti, Mufulira and Ndola are told to wait for two good rains, with a planting window expected around 20 to 26 November.

At the other end of the scale, 42 districts are simply told to wait: all of Lusaka and Southern provinces, most of Central and Eastern, and Mwandi and Sesheke in Western, where little rain is expected through 26 November. Kabwe, Chama, Chasefu and Mongu are told to hold off because a dry spell is likely. The bulletin also addresses the 15 districts, mostly in Southern and Lusaka, that had a false start in early October: farmers who planted then should not replant after the next isolated shower but wait until their district is marked Plant.

body.text: A season that may be short

body: The longer-range warning is the one that matters for the maize crop. The Monitor reported the department saying that the El Niño-influenced season may last 90 days or less in Southern and Lusaka provinces and in the valley areas, and recommending drought-tolerant crops such as sorghum, pearl millet and cowpeas, with maize confined to a small area and to extra-early varieties, planted in two or three batches about a week apart. Afternoon temperatures of 39 to 41 degrees Celsius are forecast in the Zambezi and Luangwa valleys and around 38 degrees across the south, with Southern, Lusaka, Western and Central provinces running 3 to 5 degrees above normal, which raises evaporation, bushfire risk and heat stress.

That advice echoes what the department's senior meteorologist Peggy Thole told News Diggers in late October, when a 14-day outlook for 22 October to 4 November warned of temperatures of 41 to 44 degrees. **"They (farmers) should also look at planting various crops, not just relying on one crop,"** she said then, adding that **"some of those crops should be drought-tolerant crops"**. State House's statement on Sunday on the term-limit debate listed El Niño and food security among the President's immediate priorities. The department's own website had not yet posted the new bulletin by Monday morning; the most recent document listed there dates from March 2026.

stories.title: Musonda in the 83rd, then Chitambala with two saves: Zambia's under-23s beat Burkina Faso 1–0 at Heroes and win 3–2 on penalties to reach the final qualifying round
stories.excerpt: Trailing 1–0 from Ouagadougou, Chisi Mbewe's side needed a substitute's late goal and a goalkeeper's nerve. Caleb Musonda scored in the 83rd minute at National Heroes Stadium on Sunday 15 November to level the tie on aggregate, and Christo Chitambala saved two penalties as Zambia won the shoot-out 3–2. The reward is a two-legged final-round tie in March 2027 against the winner of Nigeria v DR Congo, with a place at the Egypt 2027 under-23 finals at stake.

image.label: Heroes, 3–2 on penalties
image.caption: A late goal and two saved penalties put the under-23s one tie away from the Egypt 2027 finals.

body: The coach had asked for two unanswered goals; his players found one, and a goalkeeper did the rest. Zambia's under-23s beat Burkina Faso 1–0 at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka on Sunday 15 November, levelling the second-round tie at 1–1 on aggregate after the 1–0 defeat in Ouagadougou, and then won the penalty shoot-out 3–2 to move into the final qualifying round for the 2027 under-23 Africa Cup of Nations. ZamFoot reported the match in detail, and the Confederation of African Football confirmed the result on its website.

According to ZamFoot, Eliya Mandanji struck the post early in the second half and the breakthrough came only in the 83rd minute, when the substitute Caleb Musonda scored. Pascal Phiri went close four minutes later, and a second goal from Mandanji was ruled out for offside. With no further scoring the tie went to penalties.

Zambia's three successful kicks came from Mandanji, Phiri and Charles Buyoya; Happy Nsiku's effort was saved. For Burkina Faso, Jack Pantoulou Diarra and Doque Seydou Fofana scored, Christo Chitambala saved from Cherif Badra Ali Barro and Fadil Adama Barro, and Cyril Dao put his kick wide. Chitambala, who ZamFoot named as the hero of the night, had Haidara Cherif as his opposite number.

Before the match the coach, Chisi Mbewe, had been blunt about the arithmetic. The Times of Zambia reported him calling it a do-or-die game and saying Zambia had to score two unanswered goals to progress; he asked supporters to fill the stadium as the crowd in Ndola had done for the senior side two days earlier. The Times noted that the fixture was the first international at Heroes in more than two years, following renovations to meet FIFA certification standards. In the end a single goal and the shoot-out were enough.

CAF's report lists Zambia among the sides already through to the final round, in which seven two-legged ties will decide the teams that join hosts Egypt at the finals; the tournament also forms part of Africa's qualifying route to men's football at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. ZamFoot reported that Zambia will meet either Nigeria or the Democratic Republic of Congo in March 2027. That tie is not yet settled: DR Congo won the first leg 2–0, according to CAF, and the return, listed as Nigeria v DR Congo, is on Tuesday 17 November. Other second legs this week include Ghana v Libya, with Ghana trailing 1–0, and Algeria's return against Eswatini on Monday 16 November after a 2–1 first-leg defeat.

stories.title: Algeria go three clear while Zambia fly south: the Chipolopolo are in Bujumbura for Tuesday's return against Burundi, with Kings Kangwa back and second place to defend
stories.excerpt: The senior side landed in Bujumbura at 12:45 on Saturday 14 November and are based at the Hotel Club du Lac Tanganyika ahead of Tuesday's Group I qualifier against Burundi. That evening Algeria beat Togo 1–0 in Tizi Ouzou through Ramy Bensebaini's 76th-minute header, moving to seven points; Zambia have four, Togo three and Burundi two. George Lwandamina says Kings Kangwa, back from a four-match suspension, is a player who can turn a game on his own.

image.label: Bujumbura, Tuesday
image.caption: Zambia take four points and a returning midfielder to Burundi, where a win would keep them second behind Algeria.

body: The day after the 1–1 draw in Ndola, the Chipolopolo were in Burundi. FAZ Media, in a report carried by ZamFoot, said the squad landed at Melchior Ndadaye International Airport in Bujumbura at 12:45 local time on Saturday 14 November and settled into the Hotel Club du Lac Tanganyika, where they will prepare for Tuesday's Group I qualifier for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations. The report did not give the kick-off time or the venue.

The group moved on without them on Saturday evening. Pan Africa Football reported that Algeria beat Togo 1–0 at the Stade Hocine-Aït-Ahmed in Tizi Ouzou, Ramy Bensebaini heading in Anis Hadj Moussa's cross in the 76th minute. That takes Algeria to seven points from three games, with Zambia on four, Togo on three and Burundi on two, according to the standings published by ZamFoot after the Ndola match and by Pan Africa Football after Saturday's game. Togo host Algeria in Lomé on Tuesday, the same day Zambia play in Bujumbura.

The main change to George Lwandamina's options is the return of Kings Kangwa, who has completed the four-match ban he received for a red card in Zambia's 3–0 defeat by Morocco at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations. ZamFoot quoted the coach after Friday's draw: **"He's a seasoned player. I'm sure he's going to add value to the team,"** Lwandamina said of Kangwa, adding: **"He's a player who can turn around the game individually. He has the brains."** He also pointed to players who missed the first leg and said he expected them to make a difference in the return, without naming them.

Of the draw itself, in which Edward Chilufya scored in the second half before Jean Claude Girumugisha equalised for Burundi in the 82nd minute, Lwandamina was brief. **"It was just a bad day. I'm sure the boys will rise,"** he told ZamFoot, saying he was disappointed to drop two points at home but confident of a response. The two points dropped in Ndola leave Zambia needing a result away to stay clear of Togo.

The arithmetic is simple enough. A win in Bujumbura would take Zambia to seven points and keep them level with Algeria if Algeria lose in Lomé, or three behind if Algeria win; a draw would leave Zambia on five, and a Togo win over Algeria in Lomé the same day would lift Togo to six and into second place. With the two sides meeting twice in four days, this is the half of the double-header that decides whether Friday's draw was a stumble or the start of a slide.

stories.title: Mama G walks the red carpet at Manda Hill: 'The Family Affair', a Zambian drama with Nollywood's Patience Ozokwor, premieres in Lusaka with Lagos, Nairobi and London to follow
stories.excerpt: Basali Media and Kazadi Films premiered 'The Family Affair' at Ster-Kinekor, Manda Hill, on Saturday 14 November. Written by Veronica Hachipuka and directed by David Kazadi, the film stars Samantha Zulu as Vanessa Milimo, a single mother diagnosed with stage-three breast cancer, with Patience Ozokwor, known across the continent as Mama G, as Mama D. Ozokwor shot her scenes in Zambia in April and returned on Friday 13 November for the premiere; the producers plan screenings in Lagos, Nairobi and London before a streaming release.

image.label: Red carpet, Manda Hill
image.caption: A Zambian-written, Zambian-directed drama with a Nollywood star opened in Lusaka before touring three other cities.

body: The Nigerian actress Patience Ozokwor, the Nollywood veteran known to audiences as Mama G, walked a red carpet at Manda Hill on Saturday 14 November for the premiere of a Zambian film in which she plays, inevitably, a formidable mother. The Zambia Monitor reported from the Ster-Kinekor cinema, where Basali Media, in association with Kazadi Films, unveiled 'The Family Affair' to an invited audience.

The film is written by Veronica Hachipuka and directed by David Kazadi. Samantha Zulu leads as Vanessa Milimo, a single mother diagnosed with stage-three breast cancer, and Ozokwor plays Mama D. The Zambian cast includes Kondwani Elliott Zulu, Lee Nonde, Mwaka Mugala, Stella Sikana and Lorna Lemi. The Monitor described the story as one of family loyalty, betrayal and the lengths people go to in order to protect those they love.

body.text: Seven months from shoot to screen

body: Ozokwor's involvement has been a long courtship. According to the Monitor, she arrived in Lusaka on 17 April to shoot her scenes and was given a send-off by the production on 2 May. On 6 October she told her followers on social media: **"I am coming to Zambia to watch 'The Family Affair' WITH YOU at the EXCLUSIVE Red-carpet premiere in Lusaka!"** She landed on Friday 13 November, was welcomed at the airport and gave a press briefing before Saturday's screening.

On the night she wore a champagne-gold gown by the Zambian designer Ejabali, and afterwards thanked the stylist and her team. **"It was, indeed, an honour to show up at the red-carpet activities fully styled by Ejabali,"** she said, in remarks reported by the Monitor.

The producers are not stopping in Lusaka. The Monitor reported that premieres are planned for Lagos, Nairobi and London, and that the film's writer and executive producer said in July that it would be released on YouTube and other streaming platforms once the premieres are done. The casting pairs a Nollywood name with a Zambian ensemble, a Zambian writer and a Zambian director, and the planned tour of three cities outside Zambia suggests the producers are aiming at an audience well beyond Lusaka.

sources.title: Glitz, glamour as Mama G headlines Zambian drama 'The Family Affair' at Lusaka premiere

analysis.title: A statement that declines to settle the one question being asked
analysis.body: State House's Sunday statement is carefully built. It does not say the President wants a third term, and it does not say he would refuse one. It says the debate belongs to citizens and that he will not be drawn. Supporters of the government can fairly point out that the executive has no formal role in a petition to Parliament, that a presidential intervention either way could be read as pressure on MPs, and that Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu has already said the Assembly is the right place for the petitions. Opponents can fairly reply that the question is not procedural but personal: the only person who can rule out benefiting from a change to the two-term limit is the man it would benefit, and Given Lubinda's challenge was framed exactly that way. Cosmas Musumali's charge of indirect endorsement rests on the same gap. What to watch is not State House but the National Assembly: whether the three petitions are tabled, which committee takes them, and whether any MP sponsors a bill. Until then the row runs on silence, and silence can be read as whichever side prefers.

analysis.title: Mpika's gold: the State is formalising with one hand and arresting with the other
analysis.body: The weekend's arrests at Muneshi Stream arrived four days after regulators sat down with Chief Chikwanda and local miners to explain how artisanal gold rights will be allocated at Kamambwe, Kanyelele and Danger Hill. The two moves are meant to work together: tenements for Zambian citizens who register, enforcement against those who dig and process without licences. The Commission's account of a site suspended two months ago and back in operation shows why the second half matters, and the suspected pollution of a stream used by villages downstream explains the involvement of ZEMA. What is still unknown is what happens next. No charges have been reported against the 20 arrested, no equipment or gold has been listed as seized, and the Immigration Department's separate action, a deportation after a shooting and 15 people held over permits, concerns different sites and different offences. Mercury use, which the provincial administration raised at the Mpika meeting, has not been confirmed at Muneshi. The test of the formalisation drive will be whether licensed Zambian miners are working these sites by the next rainy season, and whether the courts, rather than press statements, decide what the 20 did.

analysis.title: Half the normal rain in Lusaka, and a season that may be 90 days long
analysis.body: The Met Department's first bulletin confirms what the El Niño forecast implied: a split country. Northern and Luapula have had more rain than usual and may plant now; Lusaka, Southern and Central have had about half their normal total and are told to wait, with a season that could last 90 days or less. The practical advice is specific and demanding. Drought-tolerant crops, maize on a small area in extra-early varieties, planting in two or three batches a week apart, and no replanting after the false start of early October until a district is marked Plant. For smallholders who have already bought maize seed, switching part of a field to sorghum or cowpeas is not a free choice, and the advice to plant in batches assumes labour and seed to spare. For the government, which has named food security as a priority, a poor southern harvest in 2027 would be a budget problem as much as a farming one. The counter-argument is that forecasts are probabilities, that the northern half of the country has had above-average rain, and that a short season well managed can still produce a crop. What to watch is the next bulletin, due at the end of November, and whether the Copperbelt's planting window around 20 to 26 November actually opens.
